title: Spatial data analysis: week 11 tutorial
text:
Week 11 — Spatial point processes
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
In this tutorial, we analyse the spatial distribution of nests of two ant species, Messor wasmanni and Cataglyphis bicolor, recorded at a site in northern Greece. The dataset ants from the spatstat.data package contains locations of 97 ant nests within a sampling window.. You can load the data using
`data(ants)` from `spatstat.data`. `plot()` shows the pattern and `summary()`
gives the window, the number of points and the average intensity.
Look at the pattern first and form an opinion before you compute anything: does
it look clustered, regular, or neither?
library(spatstat)
library(spatstat.data)
data(ants)

summary(ants)
plot(ants, main = "Spatial Point Pattern of Ant Nests", 
     cex = 0.8, pch = c(16, 17), cols = c("red", "blue"))
legend("topright", legend = c("Cataglyphis", "Messor"), 
       pch = c(16, 17), col = c("red", "blue"))
library(spatstat)
library(spatstat.data)
data(ants)

summary(ants)
plot(ants, main = "Spatial Point Pattern of Ant Nests", 
     cex = 0.8, pch = c(16, 17), cols = c("red", "blue"))
legend("topright", legend = c("Cataglyphis", "Messor"), 
       pch = c(16, 17), col = c("red", "blue"))
This summary shows that the average intensity is 0.000226 points per square unit. The proportion of Cataglyphis nests is 29.9%, Messor 70.1%. The observation window is irregularly shaped. The plot shows two types of ant nests (Cataglyphis and Messor) distributed within a polygonal study window. Messor nests are represented by blue triangles (likely pch = 17) and Cataglyphis by red dots (pch = 16).
Two complementary views. One function divides the window into a grid and counts points per cell — crude
but easy to test. Another gives a smooth kernel estimate of the intensity
surface; it is the `ppp` method of a familiar function.
The bandwidth matters: too small and you see noise, too large and you smooth the
structure away.
Q <- quadratcount(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
print(Q)
plot(ants, main="Quadrat Count of Ant Nests")
plot(Q, add=TRUE, col="red")

lambda_hat <- density(ants, bw.diggle)
plot(lambda_hat, main="Kernel Intensity Estimate of Ant Nests")
plot(ants, add=TRUE, pch=16, cex=0.5)
Q <- quadratcount(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
print(Q)
plot(ants, main="Quadrat Count of Ant Nests")
plot(Q, add=TRUE, col="red")

lambda_hat <- density(ants, bw.diggle)
plot(lambda_hat, main="Kernel Intensity Estimate of Ant Nests")
plot(ants, add=TRUE, pch=16, cex=0.5)
The quadrat counts show considerable variation in nest counts across quadrats. Some quadrats have 0 nests while others have up to 9. This suggests possible spatial inhomogeneity ### Kernel intensity estimation Let’s estimate the spatial intensity using kernel smoothing: The intensity surface shows spatial variability, with hotspots where ant nests are more concentrated. The Diggle bandwidth selector automatically chose an appropriate smoothing parameter
`ppm(ants, ~1)` fits a homogeneous Poisson process — constant intensity, points
independent. `ppm(ants, ~ x + y)` lets the log intensity vary linearly across
the window.
The second is still a Poisson process: points remain independent given the
intensity. Only the first-order structure has changed.
ppm_hom <- ppm(ants, ~1)
summary(ppm_hom)

ppm_inhom <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y)
summary(ppm_inhom)
ppm_hom <- ppm(ants, ~1)
summary(ppm_hom)

ppm_inhom <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y)
summary(ppm_inhom)
Key points are as follows: - The model assumes constant intensity across the study area - The estimated intensity is 0.000113 nests per square unit for each species - The log intensity is -9.087 with SE 0.102 - This is the simplest model, assuming no spatial trends ### Inhomogeneous Poisson process with coordinates as covariates Now we fit a model with spatial trend using x and y coordinates: Key points are as follows: - The model includes linear trends in x and y directions - Neither x nor y coefficients are statistically significant (p-values > 0.05) - The model suggests weak spatial trends at best
There is a test that compares observed and expected counts per quadrat. A small
p-value says the homogeneous Poisson model does not fit — but it will not tell
you whether the cause is a trend in intensity or genuine interaction between
points.
quadrat.test(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
quadrat.test(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
\(\chi^2\) = 18.512, df = 23, p-value = 0.5417 suggesting that the test does not reject CSR. However, this doesn’t account for possible inhomogeneity

title: Spatial data analysis: week 11 tutorial
text:
Challenge










`Kest()` estimates Ripley's K, and `envelope()` gives simulation bounds under
complete spatial randomness.
Above the theoretical line means clustering, below means regularity. Ant nests
compete for space, so think about which you would expect before you look.




par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Compute the K-function with Ripley correction
Kc <- Kest(ants, correction = "Ripley")

# Plot the envelope of the K-function (simulations under CSR)
plot(envelope(ants, Kest, nsim = 100), main = "K function with Envelope")

# Plot the centered K-function (difference between estimated and theoretical K)
plot(Kc$r, Kc$iso - Kc$theo, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Compute the K-function with Ripley correction
Kc <- Kest(ants, correction = "Ripley")

# Plot the envelope of the K-function (simulations under CSR)
plot(envelope(ants, Kest, nsim = 100), main = "K function with Envelope")

# Plot the centered K-function (difference between estimated and theoretical K)
plot(Kc$r, Kc$iso - Kc$theo, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")


The observed K-function (black line) mostly falls within the CSR envelope. Some slight deviation at intermediate distances (50-100 units). There is no strong evidence of clustering or regularity. The pattern is generally consistent with CSR ### Challenge

Fit a model with a quadratic trend surface using x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2) as covariates. Compare it with the linear model.











`ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))`. The `I()` is needed so `^` means power
rather than formula-crossing.
Compare with the linear-trend fit using `AIC()`. A quadratic surface can capture
a ridge or a hollow that a plane cannot.




ppm_quad <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))
summary(ppm_quad)

AIC(ppm_inhom)
AIC(ppm_quad)
ppm_quad <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))
summary(ppm_quad)

AIC(ppm_inhom)
AIC(ppm_quad)


The quadratic terms are not statistically significant. AIC for linear model: 1961.509 and AIC for quadratic model: 1964.004. The simpler linear model is preferred (lower AIC)

Simulate 99 point patterns from your best model and compare their envelope with the observed K-function using envelope().











The same envelope function you used in item 5 accepts a *fitted model* in place
of the point pattern, in which case it simulates from that model rather than
from complete spatial randomness. That is the sharper test: it asks whether
anything is left unexplained once the trend is accounted for.
If the observed K now sits inside the envelope, the inhomogeneity explained the
apparent clustering.




if (AIC(ppm_quad) < AIC(ppm_inhom)) {
  best_model <- ppm_quad
} else {
  best_model <- ppm_inhom
}
envelope_obj <- envelope(best_model, Kest, nsim=99, rank=1, verbose=FALSE)
plot(envelope_obj, main="Envelope of K-function with Simulations")
abline(a=pi, b=0, col="red", lty=2)

plot(envelope_obj$r, envelope_obj$obs - envelope_obj$mmean, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
if (AIC(ppm_quad) < AIC(ppm_inhom)) {
  best_model <- ppm_quad
} else {
  best_model <- ppm_inhom
}
envelope_obj <- envelope(best_model, Kest, nsim=99, rank=1, verbose=FALSE)
plot(envelope_obj, main="Envelope of K-function with Simulations")
abline(a=pi, b=0, col="red", lty=2)

plot(envelope_obj$r, envelope_obj$obs - envelope_obj$mmean, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")


The observed K-function remains within the simulation envelope. The quadratic terms didn’t improve model fit. The spatial pattern is well-described by CSR or simple linear trend.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 11 tutorial
text:
Week 11 complete




What you have learnt
You have analysed the third type of spatial data, where the locations themselves are the random quantity.

A different question. For geostatistical and areal data the locations are given and the values are random. For a point pattern the locations are the data, and the question is whether they are clustered, regular or random.
First-order versus second-order. Intensity is how many points per unit area and how that varies across the window; interaction is whether points attract or repel each other. They are genuinely different, and are easily confused.
Complete spatial randomness is the homogeneous Poisson process, and it is the null against which everything else is judged.
Quadrat tests are simple but blunt: a small p-value tells you the homogeneous Poisson model fails without saying whether the cause is a trend in intensity or interaction between points.
Ripley’s K with a simulation envelope separates the two. Above the theoretical curve suggests clustering, below suggests regularity.
The important subtlety. Fitting an inhomogeneous Poisson process and then re-testing with an envelope simulated from that model asks whether anything is left once the trend is accounted for. Apparent clustering often turns out to be a varying intensity rather than interaction — the classic confounding of first and second order.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Week 9 — Areal data and Moran’s I
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Lip cancer data in scotland. The data contain, for each of the Scotland counties, the number of observed and expected lip cancer cases among males in Scotland between 1975-1980, and a variable that indicates the proportion of the population engaged in agriculture, fishing, or forestry (aff). The aff variable is related to exposure to sunlight which is a risk factor for lip cancer. The data also contain the shapefile of the Scotland counties and everything can be found in scotland_lip
`data(scotland_lip)` — it is already an `sf` object, so the geometry comes with
it. Look at the columns before going on.
# Read shapefile (make sure the .shp, .dbf, .shx files are all present)
scot <- scotland_lip

# View structure of the dataset
glimpse(scot)
# Read shapefile (make sure the .shp, .dbf, .shx files are all present)
scot <- scotland_lip

# View structure of the dataset
glimpse(scot)
This shapefile includes Scotland counties with observed (observed) and expected (expected) lip cancer counts and an aff variable.
The SIR is observed over expected. There is a helper: `sir(cases, expected)`.
A value above 1 means more cases than the age-sex structure of that county would
predict. Map it with a diverging scale centred on 1, so above and below are
visually distinct.
scot$SIR <- scot$cases / scot$expected

# Plot SIR using tmap
tm_shape(scot) +
  tm_fill("SIR", style = "quantile", palette = "YlOrRd", title = "SIR") +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Standardized Incidence Ratios (SIR) in Scotland")
scot$SIR <- scot$cases / scot$expected

# Plot SIR using tmap
tm_shape(scot) +
  tm_fill("SIR", style = "quantile", palette = "YlOrRd", title = "SIR") +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Standardized Incidence Ratios (SIR) in Scotland")
Red color correspond to higher SIRs, i.e., higher-than-expected lip cancer cases. Counties with SIR > 1 (darker red areas) have a higher-than-expected incidence. This could suggest localized risk factors, possibly linked to environmental or occupational exposure.
Scatter plot of SIR against `aff`. AFF is a proxy for outdoor work and hence
sunlight exposure, which is a known risk factor for lip cancer — so a positive
slope is the expected direction.
ggplot(scot, aes(x = aff, y = SIR)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "SIR vs. aff", x = "Proportion in aff", y = "SIR")
ggplot(scot, aes(x = aff, y = SIR)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "SIR vs. aff", x = "Proportion in aff", y = "SIR")
The scatter shows the plot with SIR on the y-axis and aff (proportion in agriculture, fishing, or forestry) on the x-axis. A regression line (in red) with a slight upward slope. There appears to be a weak positive association: counties with more people in aff-related jobs may have higher SIRs. This is consistent with the hypothesis that sun exposure (common in those occupations) might be linked to lip cancer risk.However, the spread is large, and correlation may not be strong without further statistical testing.
`spdep` builds a neighbour list straight from polygons. Its `queen` argument
decides the rule: `TRUE` counts a shared corner as adjacency, `FALSE` requires a
shared edge.
Scotland has islands. If a region ends up with no neighbours, that is a real
feature of the geography, not a bug — though `snap` can bridge small gaps.
nb_queen <- poly2nb(scot, queen = TRUE)
neighbor_counts <- card(nb_queen)
data.frame(county = scot$county , no_neigbours = neighbor_counts)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_queen, st_geometry(scot), main = "Queen Contiguity Neighbors", add = TRUE)
nb_queen <- poly2nb(scot, queen = TRUE)
neighbor_counts <- card(nb_queen)
data.frame(county = scot$county , no_neigbours = neighbor_counts)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_queen, st_geometry(scot), main = "Queen Contiguity Neighbors", add = TRUE)
Most counties have more than one neighbors, some with zero. The map shows the connectedness of the counties and these are essential for defining spatial weights and for modeling spatial dependence.
`card()` gives the number of neighbours per region. Find the maximum and which
county attains it.
max_n <- max(neighbor_counts)
most_connected <- scot$county[which(neighbor_counts == max_n)]
most_connected
max_n <- max(neighbor_counts)
most_connected <- scot$county[which(neighbor_counts == max_n)]
most_connected
The county with the largest number of neigbours is Perth-Kinross.
Find Wigtown's index, pull its neighbours out of the neighbour list, then map
the three categories: the county itself, its neighbours, and everywhere else.
wigtown_index <- which(scot$county == "wigtown")
wigtown_nb <- nb_queen[[wigtown_index]]
scot$neighbors <- "other"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_index] <- "area"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_nb] <- "neighbors"
ggplot(scot) + geom_sf(aes(fill = neighbors)) + theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "gray", "white"))
wigtown_index <- which(scot$county == "wigtown")
wigtown_nb <- nb_queen[[wigtown_index]]
scot$neighbors <- "other"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_index] <- "area"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_nb] <- "neighbors"
ggplot(scot) + geom_sf(aes(fill = neighbors)) + theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "gray", "white"))
A map shows Wigtown and its neighboring counties.
`nb2mat()` with `style = "B"` for binary and `style = "W"` for row-standardised.
Row-standardised means each row sums to one, so a region with many neighbours
gives each of them less weight.
Islands with no neighbours need `zero.policy = TRUE`.
W_binary <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_binary[1:10, 1:10]

W_rowstd <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_rowstd[1:10, 1:10]
W_binary <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_binary[1:10, 1:10]

W_rowstd <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_rowstd[1:10, 1:10]

title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Challenge










Convert the neighbour list into a weights list object first, then pass it to
the Moran's I test function.
Positive Moran's I means nearby counties have similar SIRs. Check the p-value,
but also look at the statistic against its expectation, which is -1/(n-1) rather
than zero.




# Create spatial weights list
lw <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
moran.test(scot$SIR, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
# Create spatial weights list
lw <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
moran.test(scot$SIR, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


Moran’s I is highly significant (p < 0.000001), indicating strong spatial autocorrelation in SIR. In plain terms: counties with high SIR tend to be near other counties with high SIR, and same for low SIR. This validates the need to account for spatial structure in modeling cancer risk. ## Challenge

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on 3 nearest neighbors and map the neighbors obtained.











Two steps: find the k nearest centroids, then convert that to a neighbour list
with `knn2nb()`. Note this gives every region exactly three neighbours,
including the islands — which is either a feature or a distortion,
depending on what you think adjacency should mean.




coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(scot))
knn3 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 3)
nb_knn3 <- knn2nb(knn3)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_knn3, coords, main = "3-Nearest Neighbor Connectivity", add = T)
coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(scot))
knn3 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 3)
nb_knn3 <- knn2nb(knn3)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_knn3, coords, main = "3-Nearest Neighbor Connectivity", add = T)


Each county is connected to its 3 closest neighbors by distance. Useful when physical proximity is more important than shared boundaries (e.g., for air pollution, etc.).

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on distance and map the neighbors obtained.











The distance-based constructor in `spdep` takes a lower and an upper bound. The geometry is in
metres, so the bounds must be too.




dists <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 50)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(dists, coords, main = "Distance-Based Neighbors", add= T)
dists <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 50)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(dists, coords, main = "Distance-Based Neighbors", add= T)


Counties within the distance of 50 to each other are connected. Allows flexible neighborhood structures based on absolute proximity. May capture spatial spillover more naturally than contiguity in some contexts.

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on contiguity Neighbors of order 2 and map the neighbors obtained.











There is a `spdep` function for higher-order (lagged) neighbours. Order 2 means "neighbours of my
neighbours", which widens the definition of local considerably.




nb_order2 <- nblag(nb_queen, 2)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_order2[[2]], coords, main = "Second-Order Queen Neighbors", add = T)
nb_order2 <- nblag(nb_queen, 2)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_order2[[2]], coords, main = "Second-Order Queen Neighbors", add = T)


This visualizes neighbors-of-neighbors.

Construct the spatial weights matrix using inverse distance values.











Compute inverse distances between centroids, then pass them to `nb2mat()` via
`glist`. Closer neighbours then carry more weight than distant ones.




distances <- nbdists(nb_queen, coords)
inv_dists <- lapply(distances, function(x) 1/x)
lw_inv <- nb2mat(nb_queen, glist = inv_dists, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw_inv[1:10, 1:10]
distances <- nbdists(nb_queen, coords)
inv_dists <- lapply(distances, function(x) 1/x)
lw_inv <- nb2mat(nb_queen, glist = inv_dists, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw_inv[1:10, 1:10]


We are showing a few rows and columns of the spatial weight matrix based on inverse distance. Closer neighbors have more influence, farther ones less.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Week 9 complete




What you have learnt
You have moved from point-referenced to area-level data, where “nearby” has to be defined rather than measured.

Standardised incidence ratios. Observed over expected, so a value above 1 is more cases than the population structure predicts. SIRs based on small expected counts are extremely noisy — which is exactly the problem CAR models solve next week.
Adjacency is a modelling choice. Queen or rook contiguity, k nearest neighbours, a distance threshold, or higher-order lags. Each encodes a different idea of what makes two areas neighbours, and each gives different answers.
Islands are real. Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles have no contiguous neighbours at all. You either bridge them with a snapping tolerance, use a distance or k-nearest rule, or handle empty neighbour sets explicitly.
Weights matrices. Binary treats all neighbours alike; row-standardised gives each area’s neighbours equal total influence, so an area with many neighbours weights each one less.
Moran’s I. A global test for spatial autocorrelation. Note its expectation under the null is \(-1/(n-1)\), not zero.

The point to hold on to: every one of these results depends on the weights matrix you chose. Report that choice as part of the analysis.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 7 tutorial
text:
Week 7 — Geostatistics and variograms
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Galicia dataset, often used in geostatistical analysis, refers to lead concentration data from a network of meteorological stations across the Galicia region in Northwest Spain. The Galicia dataset has the following columns:
`data(galicia)`. Five columns: the lead concentration and its log, the
coordinates, and PM10. Check which is which before you go further — you will be
modelling the log, not the raw concentration.
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# View the first few rows
head(galicia)
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# View the first few rows
head(galicia)
The dataset contains 5 variables: - lead: measured lead concentration - loglead: log-transformed lead - long, lat: geographic coordinates - pm10: pollutant levels This is the basic EDA (exploratory data analysis) step. Always check variable types and completeness first.
Turn the data frame into an `sf` object with `st_as_sf()`, telling it which
columns hold the coordinates and what CRS they are in (these are longitude and
latitude, so EPSG:4326).
Then map it. When you look at the map, ask where the stations are — is the
design regular, clustered, or opportunistic? That governs what you can estimate.
# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

# Map the lead concentration
tm_shape(galicia_sf) +
  tm_symbols(col = "lead", palette = "viridis", style = "quantile",
             title.col = "Lead conc.") +
  tm_layout(title = "")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = galicia_sf, aes(color = lead), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Lead Concentration in Galicia", color = "Lead") +
  theme_minimal()
# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

# Map the lead concentration
tm_shape(galicia_sf) +
  tm_symbols(col = "lead", palette = "viridis", style = "quantile",
             title.col = "Lead conc.") +
  tm_layout(title = "")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = galicia_sf, aes(color = lead), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Lead Concentration in Galicia", color = "Lead") +
  theme_minimal()
Converts the data to a spatial object and plots spatial locations with colors indicating lead concentration. I have provided two ways of mapping the data, you can always use the one that you found interesting and easy.
An ordinary scatter plot of `loglead` against `pm10`, with a fitted line.
Both are products of traffic and industry, so a positive association would not
be surprising.
ggplot(galicia, aes(x = pm10, y = loglead)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of log(lead) vs PM10", x = "PM10", y = "Log(Lead)") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(galicia, aes(x = pm10, y = loglead)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of log(lead) vs PM10", x = "PM10", y = "Log(Lead)") +
  theme_minimal()
If there’s a visible trend and a linear fit, then PM10 is a meaningful predictor. In your case, a clear positive trend suggests so.
Fit `lm(loglead ~ pm10)` first, then build the variogram of its **residuals** —
not of the raw response. The variogram of the response would confound spatial
structure with the trend the covariate explains.
Add a Monte Carlo envelope so you can judge whether the shape is more than noise.
lm1 <- lm(loglead ~ pm10, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid <- residuals(lm1)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)

galicia_variog <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
lm1 <- lm(loglead ~ pm10, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid <- residuals(lm1)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)

galicia_variog <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
A variogram shows how data points are correlated over distance. After removing the effect of PM10 (via regression), we assess the spatial structure in residuals. The variogram rises with distance, meaning that there’s spatial correlation. The envelope via permutation helps confirm if observed structure is statistically significant. In this case, the observed spatial correlation is significant as the some of the empirical semi-variogram (dots) lies outside the Monte Carlo envelopes.

Compare the two variograms. If removing the covariate makes the variogram rise
more steeply, the covariate was explaining part of what otherwise looks like
spatial correlation.

galicia_sf$resid2 <- residuals(lm2)

galicia_variog2 <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid2",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)

is as good as the real one.

spatial correlation. Try changing the number of permutations and see how stable

In this example, because our outcome is prevalence data, we used logistic regression with a binomial distribution. We first assessed the effect of the available predictors and then identified the most relevant subset of predictors for the model using stepwise regression. The results showed that accounting for the selected predictors substantially reduced the underlying spatial correlation in the residuals.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 7 tutorial
text:
Week 7 complete




What you have learnt
You have made the jump from time to space, and met the tool that detects spatial correlation.

Geostatistical data. Measurements at a finite set of locations, of a quantity that exists everywhere. That is what makes prediction at unobserved locations a sensible thing to ask for.
Design matters. Looking at the map of stations tells you what the data can support. Few close pairs means little information at short range — which will come back in week 8 when the nugget turns out to be unidentifiable.
The variogram. Half the mean squared difference between pairs, as a function of the distance between them. Rising then flattening is the signature of spatial correlation.
Always on residuals. You built the variogram from the residuals of a model with the covariate, not from the raw response. A trend left in the data looks like spatial correlation and will inflate the variogram.
Removing the covariate changed the variogram, which tells you PM10 was explaining part of what would otherwise have been attributed to space.
The Monte Carlo envelope test. Permuting values across locations destroys any spatial structure while keeping the marginal distribution. If the observed variogram sits outside the envelope, location matters.

The link back to the first half of the unit: AR(1) in time and the exponential covariance in space are the same idea with a different index.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 4 tutorial
text:
Week 4 complete




What you have learnt
You have moved from Gaussian responses to counts, and from GLMs to GLMMs.

Why a GLM is not enough. Fitting a Poisson GLM to repeated seizure counts treats all 236 observations as independent when they come from 59 patients. The estimates may be reasonable; the standard errors are not.
The exponential family and the log link. For a Poisson model each coefficient is a log rate ratio, so exp(coef) is a multiplicative effect on the expected count.
Factor versus numeric time. Treating period as a factor lets each period have its own effect instead of assuming a straight line in period number — a weaker and often more honest assumption.
GLMMs by penalised quasi-likelihood. Adding a patient-specific random intercept accounts for patients who simply seize more than the covariates predict. Notice what happened to the standard errors.
Subject-specific interpretation. Unlike the GEE you meet next week, a GLMM coefficient describes a change for a given patient, not for the population average. For a non-linear link those are genuinely different quantities.

title: Longitudinal data analysis: week 2 tutorial
text:
Week 2 — Linear mixed models
Q1: For the fev1 data, consider a linear mixed model of the form [ ( ){ij} = 0 + 1 {ij} + b{0i} + b{1i} {ij} + {ij}, ] where \(\log\left( \frac{\text{FEV}_1}{\text{Height}} \right)_{ij}\): the response for individual \(i\) at time \(j\) \(\beta_0\): fixed intercept \(\beta_1\): fixed slope for age \(b_{0i}\): random intercept for individual \(i\), capturing between-subject variation \(b_{1i}\): random slope for age for individual \(i\) \(\varepsilon_{ij}\): within-subject residual error. Note that \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) and \(\varepsilon_{i}) \sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\).
Write the \(n_i\) observations on girl \(i\) as a vector and stack the fixed and random parts:
\[\mathbf{Y}_i = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{b}_i + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,
\qquad i = 1,\dots,m,\]
where, for girl \(i\) measured at ages \(a_{i1},\dots,a_{in_i}\):
Marginally, integrating out the random effects,
\[\mathbf{Y}_i \sim N_{n_i}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta},\;
\mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf{R}_i\right).\]
This is the key point of the whole model: correlation between two measurements on the same girl arises from two sources — the shared random effects \(\mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\), and any serial correlation in \(\mathbf{R}_i\). Measurements on different girls are independent, because they share neither.
Note that \(n_i\) varies between girls: the data are unbalanced, so the matrices differ in dimension from one girl to the next. This is why the model is written per subject rather than as one \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \dots\) for the whole sample.
`groupedData()` first: it tells `nlme` which column identifies the subject, so
`logfev1_ht ~ age | id`.
Then one `lme()` per structure. The mean model and `random =` stay the same
throughout — only `correlation =` changes. The four structures you need all have constructors in `nlme` whose names begin
`cor`. Independence is the absence of a `correlation` argument; for the other
three see `?corClasses`. ARMA needs both its orders given.
Use `method = "ML"`, because you are about to compare models that differ in
their fixed or covariance structure.
library(nlme)
dg <- groupedData(logfev1_ht ~ age | id, data = fev1)

# Compare R_i structures with a random intercept only. Adding a random slope
# here stops AR(1) and ARMA(1,1) converging -- see the explanation below.
fit_ind    <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, random = ~ 1 | id, data = dg, method = "ML")
fit_cs     <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
fit_ar1    <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id))
fit_arma11 <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corARMA(form = ~ 1 | id, p = 1, q = 1))

round(fixef(fit_ind), 4)
round(fixef(fit_ar1), 4)
library(nlme)
dg <- groupedData(logfev1_ht ~ age | id, data = fev1)

# Compare R_i structures with a random intercept only. Adding a random slope
# here stops AR(1) and ARMA(1,1) converging -- see the explanation below.
fit_ind    <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, random = ~ 1 | id, data = dg, method = "ML")
fit_cs     <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
fit_ar1    <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id))
fit_arma11 <- update(fit_ind, correlation = corARMA(form = ~ 1 | id, p = 1, q = 1))

round(fixef(fit_ind), 4)
round(fixef(fit_ar1), 4)
Four models differing only in correlation. update() avoids retyping the call, so the one thing that changes stays visible.
The two sets of fixed effects printed at the end are almost identical. Changing the assumed error correlation barely moves the estimates; it moves the standard errors. That is the same lesson GEE makes explicit in week 5.
One thing worth knowing, because it will bite you if you try it. The question specifies a random intercept and a random slope, but fitting random = ~ age | id together with corAR1 or corARMA fails to converge on these data. That is not a bug in your code: a random slope already makes the marginal correlation change with the gap between visits, and AR(1) errors do the same thing, so the two compete to explain the same structure and the likelihood has no well-identified maximum. Comparing R_i structures with the simpler G, then choosing G afterwards, avoids the problem — which is exactly why the tutorial splits the selection into two stages.
where the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.
`AIC()` and `BIC()` both accept several fitted models at once and return a table.
Lower is better for both. If they disagree, remember BIC penalises extra
parameters harder.
round(data.frame(
  AIC = c(AIC(fit_ind), AIC(fit_cs), AIC(fit_ar1), AIC(fit_arma11)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit_ind), BIC(fit_cs), BIC(fit_ar1), BIC(fit_arma11)),
  row.names = c("independent", "compound symmetry", "AR(1)", "ARMA(1,1)")), 1)
round(data.frame(
  AIC = c(AIC(fit_ind), AIC(fit_cs), AIC(fit_ar1), AIC(fit_arma11)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit_ind), BIC(fit_cs), BIC(fit_ar1), BIC(fit_arma11)),
  row.names = c("independent", "compound symmetry", "AR(1)", "ARMA(1,1)")), 1)
Both criteria are shown because they can disagree. Here they do not: AR(1) wins decisively on each, by around 400 units of AIC over independence. A gap that large is not a close call.
That result makes sense. The girls are measured roughly annually over several years, and residuals a year apart should be more alike than residuals five years apart. Compound symmetry, which forces every pair to share one correlation, scores no better than independence — it is the wrong shape for these data.
Same idea as item 3, but now `correlation =` is held at whatever you selected
and `random =` is what varies.
The three candidates are constructors whose names begin `pd` — see
`?pdClasses`. One forces equal variances and no covariance, one allows unequal
variances but still no covariance, and the general case is `nlme`'s default when
you write `random = ~ age | id`.
# AR(1) won, so hold it fixed and vary G. The general structure needs a
# different optimiser to converge here.
ctrl <- lmeControl(opt = "optim")

fit_G_ind  <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, random = pdIdent(~ age),
                  correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                  data = dg, method = "ML", control = ctrl)
fit_G_diag <- update(fit_G_ind, random = pdDiag(~ age))
fit_G_gen  <- update(fit_G_ind, random = ~ age | id)

VarCorr(fit_G_diag)
# AR(1) won, so hold it fixed and vary G. The general structure needs a
# different optimiser to converge here.
ctrl <- lmeControl(opt = "optim")

fit_G_ind  <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, random = pdIdent(~ age),
                  correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                  data = dg, method = "ML", control = ctrl)
fit_G_diag <- update(fit_G_ind, random = pdDiag(~ age))
fit_G_gen  <- update(fit_G_ind, random = ~ age | id)

VarCorr(fit_G_diag)
correlation is now fixed at AR(1) and random varies. The three G structures are nested: identity within diagonal within general.
Note control = lmeControl(opt = "optim"). With the default optimiser the general structure does not converge; switching optimisers fixes it. If a mixed model fails to converge, changing the optimiser is worth trying before concluding the model is wrong — though if several optimisers fail, that is a genuine signal of over-parameterisation.
In the printed variance components, pdDiag gives a standard deviation for the intercept and one for age but no correlation between them, because a diagonal G assumes that correlation is zero rather than estimating it.
Again, the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.
Compare the three G structures the same way you compared the R structures.
round(data.frame(
  AIC = c(AIC(fit_G_ind), AIC(fit_G_diag), AIC(fit_G_gen)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit_G_ind), BIC(fit_G_diag), BIC(fit_G_gen)),
  row.names = c("identity", "diagonal", "general")), 1)
round(data.frame(
  AIC = c(AIC(fit_G_ind), AIC(fit_G_diag), AIC(fit_G_gen)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit_G_ind), BIC(fit_G_diag), BIC(fit_G_gen)),
  row.names = c("identity", "diagonal", "general")), 1)
The same comparison for the between-subject structure.
Read this cautiously. A criterion ranks models; it does not tell you a parameter is real. If the general structure wins narrowly, check whether the extra covariance it estimates has a confidence interval that excludes zero before claiming girls who start higher also grow faster.
–>
`summary()` on the winning fit. Read three things: the fixed effects (what is
the average growth rate?), the random effects table (how much do girls differ in
intercept and slope?), and the residual standard deviation.
Try to state each in a sentence about lung function, not about the model.
summary(fit_G_diag)
summary(fit_G_diag)
The summary is the payoff. Three things to read.
Fixed effects. The coefficient on age is the population-average annual change in log(FEV1/height). It is positive, which is lung function growing through adolescence, as it should.
Random effects. The between-girl standard deviations, compared with the residual standard deviation below them. If the intercept SD is comparable to or larger than the residual SD, girls differ from one another about as much as a single girl varies between visits — which is what makes the mixed model worthwhile.
Correlation structure. The estimated AR(1) parameter Phi. A value well above zero says residuals remain related from one visit to the next even after the random effects have absorbed the between-girl differences.
When you write this up, state each of these in a sentence about lung function rather than about the model.

title: Longitudinal data analysis: week 2 tutorial
text:
Week 2 complete




What you have learnt
You have fitted linear mixed models and chosen between covariance structures.

Two sources of within-subject correlation. Shared random effects (\(\mathbf{Z}_i \mathbf{G} \mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\)) and serial correlation in the errors (\(\mathbf{R}_i\)). The marginal covariance is their sum.
Structures for \(\mathbf{R}_i\). Independence, compound symmetry (all pairs equally correlated), AR(1) (geometric decay with the gap) and ARMA(1,1). The choice is a claim about how correlation behaves over time, not a technicality.
Structures for \(\mathbf{G}\). Identity, diagonal and general — increasingly permissive about how subjects vary in intercept and slope, and whether those two are related.
Choosing between them with AIC and BIC, remembering that BIC penalises extra parameters harder, so the two can disagree.
Interpretation. A fitted mixed model tells you both the population average trajectory and how much individuals depart from it.

Worth trying: run_app("cov_explorer") to see what each structure actually looks like as a matrix and as simulated trajectories.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 1 tutorial
text:
Week 1 — Exploring longitudinal data
Q1: This question relates to the cattle data, available in the course package as cattle.
The datasets come with the course package rather than as files, so you want
`data()`, not `read.table()`. Afterwards, `dim()` and `head()` tell you the
shape and the first few rows.
data(cattle)
dim(cattle)
head(cattle[, 1:5])
data(cattle)
dim(cattle)
head(cattle[, 1:5])
60 rows and 12 columns: one row per animal, the first column the treatment group and the remaining eleven the weights. Every animal has all eleven, so the design is balanced — which is what lets us treat the data as a 60 by 11 matrix at all.
`cattle` is in wide format: one row per animal, one column per time. So a
"spaghetti plot" means drawing one line per row.
Start the plot with the first animal using `type = "l"`, then add the rest in a
loop with `lines()`. Set `ylim` from the whole dataset so no trajectory is cut
off, and remember column 1 is the group indicator, not a weight.
time <- 1:11
matplot(time, t(cattle[, -1]), type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey40",
        xlab = "Time", ylab = "Weight (kg)", main = "All 60 animals")
time <- 1:11
matplot(time, t(cattle[, -1]), type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey40",
        xlab = "Time", ylab = "Weight (kg)", main = "All 60 animals")
Each line is one animal. Two things are worth noticing. Weight increases steadily for everyone, so there is a clear time trend. And the lines stay roughly parallel: animals that start heavy stay heavy. That persistent ordering is the within-subject correlation, and it is why treating these 660 measurements as independent would be wrong.
All three summaries operate on the weight columns only, so drop the group
column first with `cattle[, -1]`.
`sapply()` applies `mean` down each column; `cov()` and `cor()` take the whole
matrix at once.
means <- colMeans(cattle[, -1])
round(means, 1)
round(cor(cattle[, -1]), 2)
means <- colMeans(cattle[, -1])
round(means, 1)
round(cor(cattle[, -1]), 2)
The means rise steadily with time, as the plot suggested.
In the correlation matrix, read along any row. Correlation is high next to the diagonal — adjacent times are near 0.9 — and falls away as the gap widens, down to around 0.5 between the first and last times. That decay with lag is the pattern AR(1) is built for, and it is why compound symmetry, which forces every pair to share one correlation, would fit these data badly.
`pairs()` draws the full scatterplot matrix in one call. Again, exclude the
group column.
Look along the diagonals: how does the spread change as the gap between two time
points grows?
pairs(cattle[, c(2, 3, 7, 12)], main = "Weights at times 1, 2, 6 and 11")
pairs(cattle[, c(2, 3, 7, 12)], main = "Weights at times 1, 2, 6 and 11")
Four times are shown rather than all eleven, because an 11 by 11 grid of panels is unreadable. The panels for adjacent times are tight, near-linear clouds; those for widely separated times are much more diffuse. This is the same information as the correlation matrix, seen directly.
`which(cattle[, 1] == 0)` gives the row numbers for one group. Use that to
subset, then repeat everything from item 4 on each group separately.
Two plots side by side is `par(mfcol = c(1, 2))`.
A <- cattle[cattle$group == 0, -1]
B <- cattle[cattle$group == 1, -1]
rbind(A = colMeans(A), B = colMeans(B))
A <- cattle[cattle$group == 0, -1]
B <- cattle[cattle$group == 1, -1]
rbind(A = colMeans(A), B = colMeans(B))
Group A starts heavier. By the last time point the two groups have converged and crossed over, so the difference between them is not constant — it changes with time. A model with only a group effect could not represent that; you need an interaction between group and time, which is what you fit in week 3.
You already have the two group subsets from item 6, so this is `pairs()` twice.
Give each a `main` title so you can tell them apart.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
pairs(A[, c(1, 2, 6, 11)], main = "Group A")
pairs(B[, c(1, 2, 6, 11)], main = "Group B")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
pairs(A[, c(1, 2, 6, 11)], main = "Group A")
pairs(B[, c(1, 2, 6, 11)], main = "Group B")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
The correlation structure looks similar in both groups: the same tightening near the diagonal and loosening away from it. That matters for modelling, because it means one covariance structure can reasonably be assumed to hold for both groups rather than fitting each separately.
Plot the first group's means with `plot()`, then add the second with `lines()`
in a different colour. Both means are vectors of length 11 that you computed in
item 6.
plot(time, colMeans(A), type = "b", pch = 16, ylim = range(cattle[, -1]),
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Mean weight (kg)")
lines(time, colMeans(B), type = "b", pch = 17, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("Group A", "Group B"), pch = c(16, 17),
       col = c("black", "red"), bty = "n")
plot(time, colMeans(A), type = "b", pch = 16, ylim = range(cattle[, -1]),
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Mean weight (kg)")
lines(time, colMeans(B), type = "b", pch = 17, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("Group A", "Group B"), pch = c(16, 17),
       col = c("black", "red"), bty = "n")
The two mean curves cross. Group A is heavier at first, its growth flattens after about time 4, and group B overtakes it. This crossing is the treatment effect, and it is a difference in slope rather than in level.
Q2 You will work with longitudinal data on lung function growth in school-age girls from Topeka, Kansas, as part of the Six Cities Study of Air Pollution and Health. The dataset contains repeated pulmonary function measurements from 299 girls, typically enrolled around ages 6-10 and followed annually until high school graduation or loss to follow-up. The number of observations per individual ranges from 1 to 12, making the dataset unbalanced with respect to age.
At each visit, lung function was measured using simple spirometry, and the outcome of interest is the logarithm of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) to height, i.e., log(FEV1/height).
The dataset is available in the course package.
Key variables include:
`fev1` is in long format: one row per visit, not per girl. So `nrow()` is the
number of observations, and the number of girls is the number of distinct `id`
values.
data(fev1)
nrow(fev1)                 # observations
length(unique(fev1$id))    # girls
data(fev1)
nrow(fev1)                 # observations
length(unique(fev1$id))    # girls
1993 observations from 299 girls — about 6.7 visits each on average, but that average conceals a lot, as the next item shows.
Count the rows per `id`, then summarise those counts. A histogram of them shows
the shape of the follow-up.
If every girl had the same count, the data would be balanced — what do you see?
per_girl <- table(fev1$id)
summary(as.numeric(per_girl))
hist(as.numeric(per_girl), breaks = 0:12, xlab = "Visits per girl", main = "")
per_girl <- table(fev1$id)
summary(as.numeric(per_girl))
hist(as.numeric(per_girl), breaks = 0:12, xlab = "Visits per girl", main = "")
The distribution is right-skewed. Most girls have several visits, but some have only one or two. So the data are unbalanced: \(n_i\) differs between girls.
This is not a defect and does not need fixing. It does have two consequences. The design matrices differ in size between girls, so the model has to be written per subject. And a girl with two visits carries far less information than one with twelve, which is exactly what produces shrinkage in the week 3 predictions.
Draw a random sample of `id` values first, then keep only the rows belonging to
them. In `ggplot`, `group = id` is what stops the lines being joined into one
long zigzag across girls.
Set a seed so your plot is reproducible.
set.seed(123)
ids <- sample(unique(fev1$id), 50)
sub <- fev1[fev1$id %in% ids, ]
plot(sub$age, sub$logfev1_ht, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "log(FEV1 / height)")
for (i in ids) {
  g <- sub[sub$id == i, ]
  lines(g$age[order(g$age)], g$logfev1_ht[order(g$age)], col = "grey50")
}
set.seed(123)
ids <- sample(unique(fev1$id), 50)
sub <- fev1[fev1$id %in% ids, ]
plot(sub$age, sub$logfev1_ht, type = "n",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "log(FEV1 / height)")
for (i in ids) {
  g <- sub[sub$id == i, ]
  lines(g$age[order(g$age)], g$logfev1_ht[order(g$age)], col = "grey50")
}
The spaghetti plot for the unbalanced case. Compared with the cattle data, notice that the lines start and stop at different ages and have different numbers of points — that is the imbalance made visible.
There is substantial variation between girls in both level and slope, which is the motivation for allowing a random intercept and a random slope in week 2.
Group by `age` and take the mean of `logfev1_ht` within each. Plotting the
result gives the population-average growth curve.
Ages are not on a common grid, so some ages are supported by very few girls —
worth bearing in mind when you read the plot.
by_age <- aggregate(logfev1_ht ~ round(age), data = fev1, FUN = mean)
names(by_age) <- c("age", "mean_logfev1_ht")
plot(by_age, pch = 16, xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Mean log(FEV1 / height)")
by_age <- aggregate(logfev1_ht ~ round(age), data = fev1, FUN = mean)
names(by_age) <- c("age", "mean_logfev1_ht")
plot(by_age, pch = 16, xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Mean log(FEV1 / height)")
Averaging within each age gives the population-level growth curve, which rises steadily through adolescence.
Ages were rounded before averaging because girls were not measured on a common grid; without rounding, most ages would be supported by a single girl. Even so the extremes are based on few observations, so treat the ends of the curve with caution.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 1 tutorial
text:
Week 1 complete




What you have learnt
You have worked with two longitudinal datasets and seen the feature that motivates the whole unit: observations on the same subject are not independent.

A spaghetti plot shows every subject’s trajectory at once. Lines that stay ordered — heavy animals staying heavy — are correlation you can see by eye.
The sample correlation matrix over time puts a number on it. Correlation was strong between adjacent times and decayed as the gap widened. That decay is what AR(1) will model in week 2.
Balanced and unbalanced designs. The cattle data are balanced: every animal measured at the same 11 times. The FEV1 data are not — girls contribute between 1 and 12 visits at ages that do not line up. That difference changes what the design matrices look like and which methods are convenient.
Group comparisons. Splitting by treatment and comparing means over time is the crudest form of the analysis the rest of the unit does properly.

The thing to carry forward: if you analysed either dataset with ordinary linear regression, you would be assuming away the correlation you have just spent an hour looking at. The standard errors would be wrong.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 3 tutorial
text:
Week 3 — Estimation and inference
Q1: For the cattle data, use the linear mixed model with random intercept and random slope in Day: to model the bodyweight growth of cattle over the observation period, where \(\mathbf{b}_i\)=\((b_{i1},b_{i2})'\sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) with \(\mathbf{G}\) being (\(2\times 2\)) positive definite and \(\varepsilon_i=(\varepsilon_{i1},...,\varepsilon_{i11})'\sim
N_{11}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\) with \(\mathbf{R}_i\) being (\(11\times
11\)) positive definite.
`groupedData()` needs the response, the time variable and the subject
identifier: `Y ~ day | subject`. The cattle data are wide, so you will need to
reshape to long form first.
library(nlme)
data(cattle)

# wide -> long: one row per animal per day
long <- reshape(cattle, direction = "long",
                varying = list(names(cattle)[2:12]),
                v.names = "Y", timevar = "day", idvar = "subject")
long$treatment <- factor(long$group, labels = c("A", "B"))
long <- long[order(long$subject, long$day), ]

cg <- groupedData(Y ~ day | subject, data = long)
head(cg, 4)
library(nlme)
data(cattle)

# wide -> long: one row per animal per day
long <- reshape(cattle, direction = "long",
                varying = list(names(cattle)[2:12]),
                v.names = "Y", timevar = "day", idvar = "subject")
long$treatment <- factor(long$group, labels = c("A", "B"))
long <- long[order(long$subject, long$day), ]

cg <- groupedData(Y ~ day | subject, data = long)
head(cg, 4)
reshape() turns the 60 by 11 wide matrix into 660 rows, one per animal per day. groupedData() then records that subject identifies the clusters, which is what lets nlme know which rows belong together.
The scalar model is
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Day}_j + \beta_2 \text{Treatment}_i
+ \beta_3\,\text{Day}_j\!\times\!\text{Treatment}_i + b_{i1} + \text{Day}_j\, b_{i2}
+ \varepsilon_{ij}.\]
Collecting the \(11\) observations on animal \(i\) gives
\[\mathbf{Y}_i = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{b}_i
+ \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,60,\]
with the following pieces.
Response. \(\mathbf{Y}_i = (Y_{i1},\dots,Y_{i,11})^{\mathrm{T}}\), the \(11 \times 1\) vector of bodyweights for animal \(i\).
Fixed effects. \(\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(\mathbf{X}_i\) is \(11 \times 4\). Writing \(t_j\) for the \(j\)th measurement day and \(T_i \in \{0,1\}\) for the treatment indicator of animal \(i\),
\[\mathbf{X}_i = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & t_1 & T_i & t_1 T_i \\
1 & t_2 & T_i & t_2 T_i \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & t_{11} & T_i & t_{11} T_i
\end{pmatrix}.\]
Because \(T_i\) does not change within an animal, its column is constant down \(\mathbf{X}_i\). The interpretation is: \(\beta_0\) the intercept for the reference group, \(\beta_1\) its growth rate per day, \(\beta_2\) the difference in intercept between groups, and \(\beta_3\) the difference in growth rate — the parameter the experiment exists to estimate.
Random effects. \(\mathbf{b}_i = (b_{i1}, b_{i2})^{\mathrm{T}}\) is \(2 \times 1\) and
\[\mathbf{Z}_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t_1 \\ 1 & t_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & t_{11} \end{pmatrix}
\quad (11 \times 2),\]
so each animal has its own intercept and its own slope in day, drawn from
\[\mathbf{b}_i \sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G}), \qquad
\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ g_{12} & g_{22} \end{pmatrix}
\ \text{positive definite}.\]
\(\mathbf{G}\) is the between-animal covariance: \(g_{11}\) how much animals differ in starting weight, \(g_{22}\) how much they differ in growth rate, \(g_{12}\) whether the two are related.
Errors. \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \sim N_{11}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_i)\), independent of \(\mathbf{b}_i\), with \(\mathbf{R}_i\) an \(11\times 11\) positive definite matrix describing within-animal variation not explained by the random effects — measurement error plus any serial correlation.
Marginal distribution. Integrating out \(\mathbf{b}_i\),
\[\mathbf{Y}_i \sim N_{11}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta},\;
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\right), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf{R}_i.\]
Two remarks worth making explicitly:
The design here is balanced — all 60 animals are measured on the same 11 days — so \(\mathbf{X}_i\), \(\mathbf{Z}_i\) and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) have the same dimensions for every \(i\), and \(\mathbf{Z}_i\) is in fact the same matrix for all animals.
The independent structure is the default: give `lme()` no `correlation`
argument at all. Keep `random = ~ day | subject` so G stays general.
# Stage 1 compares R_i structures with a random intercept only. A random slope
# here stops ARMA(1,1) converging -- see the explanation below.
lme.ide <- lme(Y ~ day * treatment, random = ~ 1 | subject,
               data = cg, method = "ML")
round(fixef(lme.ide), 3)
# Stage 1 compares R_i structures with a random intercept only. A random slope
# here stops ARMA(1,1) converging -- see the explanation below.
lme.ide <- lme(Y ~ day * treatment, random = ~ 1 | subject,
               data = cg, method = "ML")
round(fixef(lme.ide), 3)
The four fixed effects are the intercept, the growth rate, the group difference in level, and the group difference in slope — the interaction, which is the parameter the experiment exists to estimate.
Note the random intercept only at this stage. The question specifies a random slope as well, and you will add it in item 9. Comparing R_i structures with the simpler G first is deliberate: with a random slope, ARMA(1,1) does not converge on these data, because a random slope already makes the marginal correlation depend on the gap between days and an ARMA error does the same thing. The two compete to explain one feature, and the likelihood has no clear maximum.
`update()` saves retyping the whole call — pass only what changes.
Compound symmetry means every pair of times is equally correlated, however far
apart. The `nlme` constructor for it is listed in `?corClasses`; its `form`
argument names the grouping, here `~ 1 | subject`.
lme.cs <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | subject))
round(coef(lme.cs$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 3)
lme.cs <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | subject))
round(coef(lme.cs$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 3)
Compound symmetry estimates a single correlation shared by every pair of days, however far apart. Compare it with the AR(1) estimate in the next item.
Now correlation should decay with the gap in days rather than being constant —
an autoregressive structure of order 1. Its `form` needs the time variable as
well as the grouping, so `~ day | subject`.
lme.ar1 <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ day | subject))
round(coef(lme.ar1$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 3)
lme.ar1 <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ day | subject))
round(coef(lme.ar1$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 3)
The AR(1) parameter. Correlation between residuals now decays as \(\rho^{|s-t|}\), so adjacent days are strongly related and distant days barely so — a much more plausible story for growth measurements than one constant correlation.
where the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.
The ARMA constructor needs both orders given explicitly, `p` and `q`.
There is a single function that takes several fitted `lme` objects and returns
a comparison table with AIC, BIC and likelihood ratio tests. They are nested, so the
likelihood ratio tests in that table are meaningful.
lme.arma <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corARMA(form = ~ day | subject, p = 1, q = 1))
anova(lme.ide, lme.cs, lme.ar1, lme.arma)
lme.arma <- update(lme.ide, correlation = corARMA(form = ~ day | subject, p = 1, q = 1))
anova(lme.ide, lme.cs, lme.ar1, lme.arma)
anova() on nested fits gives AIC, BIC and likelihood ratio tests together.
AR(1) and ARMA(1,1) both improve enormously on independence and compound symmetry — around 440 units of AIC. Between the two the difference is small: ARMA edges it on both criteria, but by about 7 units of AIC and only 2 of BIC, which is close to a tie.
Here you meet a practical constraint that model selection tables do not show. ARMA(1,1) cannot be fitted alongside the richer G structures you are about to compare, so continuing with it would mean abandoning the second stage entirely. AR(1) is chosen for that reason, and because BIC separates the two by almost nothing. That is a defensible decision, but it is a decision, and it belongs in the write-up rather than being made silently.
Now hold `correlation` fixed and vary `random`. The most restrictive option forces the random intercept and slope to have equal
variance and zero covariance. Look for the `pd` constructor meaning "identity".
# Stage 2: hold AR(1) and vary G. The general structure needs a different
# optimiser, and ARMA(1,1) will not fit these G structures at all.
ctrl <- lmeControl(opt = "optim")
lme.G.ident <- update(lme.ar1, random = pdIdent(~ day), control = ctrl)
round(as.numeric(VarCorr(lme.G.ident)[, "StdDev"]), 4)
# Stage 2: hold AR(1) and vary G. The general structure needs a different
# optimiser, and ARMA(1,1) will not fit these G structures at all.
ctrl <- lmeControl(opt = "optim")
lme.G.ident <- update(lme.ar1, random = pdIdent(~ day), control = ctrl)
round(as.numeric(VarCorr(lme.G.ident)[, "StdDev"]), 4)
Now the random slope appears. pdIdent is the most restrictive G: equal variances for intercept and slope, and no covariance between them.
control = lmeControl(opt = "optim") switches optimiser. With the default the general structure does not converge here. If a mixed model fails to converge, trying another optimiser is a reasonable first step — but if several fail, treat that as evidence the model is asking too much of the data rather than a technical nuisance.
The next-least-restrictive option allows different variances but still no
covariance between the random intercept and slope — a diagonal G.
lme.G.diag <- update(lme.ar1, random = pdDiag(~ day), control = ctrl)
round(as.numeric(VarCorr(lme.G.diag)[, "StdDev"]), 4)
lme.G.diag <- update(lme.ar1, random = pdDiag(~ day), control = ctrl)
round(as.numeric(VarCorr(lme.G.diag)[, "StdDev"]), 4)
pdDiag allows the intercept and slope to have different variances but still forces their covariance to zero. The two standard deviations printed are on quite different scales, because one is a weight and the other a weight per day.
Again, the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.
The general structure is the unrestricted one you already fitted. Compare all
three with `anova()`.
lme.G.gen <- update(lme.ar1, random = ~ day | subject, control = ctrl)
anova(lme.G.ident, lme.G.diag, lme.G.gen)
lme.G.gen <- update(lme.ar1, random = ~ day | subject, control = ctrl)
anova(lme.G.ident, lme.G.diag, lme.G.gen)
The three G structures are nested, so the likelihood ratio tests in this table are meaningful.
If the diagonal structure is not clearly beaten by the general one, prefer it: the extra covariance parameter is buying little, and a simpler G is easier to interpret and more stable to fit.
Refit with `method = "REML"`. ML underestimates variance components because it
ignores the degrees of freedom used estimating the fixed effects; REML corrects
for that. Now that the structure is settled, REML gives better variance
estimates.
Try `run_app("lmm_simulator")` with a small number of subjects to watch this
happen.
final <- update(lme.G.diag, method = "REML")
round(fixef(final), 3)
final <- update(lme.G.diag, method = "REML")
round(fixef(final), 3)
Refitting with REML now that the structure is settled. ML underestimates variance components because it does not pay for having estimated the fixed effects; REML corrects that. The fixed effects barely move — it is the variance components that change.
run_app("lmm_simulator") with a small number of subjects shows this directly.
Two plots. The first is standardised residuals against fitted values — look for
constant spread. The second is a normal QQ plot of those residuals.
`plot(fit, resid(., type = "p") ~ fitted(.))` gives the first.
plot(final, resid(., type = "p") ~ fitted(.), abline = 0,
     xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Standardised residuals")
plot(final, resid(., type = "p") ~ fitted(.), abline = 0,
     xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Standardised residuals")
Standardised residuals against fitted values. You are looking for a horizontal band of roughly constant width. A funnel shape would suggest the variance grows with the mean and a transformation is needed; curvature would suggest the mean model is wrong.
distributed (for example check the qqnorm plot).
Random effects are not residuals, so the formula inside `qqnorm()` must extract
the predicted random effects rather than `resid(.)`. You are checking the
assumption b_i ~ N(0, G).
qqnorm(final, ~ ranef(.))
qqnorm(final, ~ ranef(.))
This is a different assumption from the last plot. Here you are checking \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) — that the animals are normally distributed around the population, not that the residuals are. Points close to the line support it; a few stragglers are worth identifying, since they are individual animals behaving unusually rather than individual measurements.
variance components. Explain whether or not they are significant.
One `nlme` function returns confidence intervals for the fixed effects, the
variance components and the correlation parameters together. An interval for a variance
that nearly touches zero is telling you something.
intervals(final, which = "fixed")
intervals(final, which = "fixed")
Confidence intervals for the fixed effects. The interaction is the one to read: if its interval excludes zero, the two groups genuinely differ in growth rate, which is the scientific question.
Interpret the interval, not just whether it contains zero. An interval from 0.01 to 0.9 excludes zero but is consistent with an effect too small to matter.
single figure. Comment on the plot.
Predict from the fitted model at each day for each treatment group, then plot
the two curves together. The gap between them is the treatment effect.
days <- sort(unique(cg$day))
nd <- expand.grid(day = days, treatment = factor(c("A", "B")))
nd$fit <- predict(final, newdata = nd, level = 0)
plot(nd$day[nd$treatment == "A"], nd$fit[nd$treatment == "A"], type = "b",
     pch = 16, ylim = range(nd$fit), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Predicted weight (kg)")
lines(nd$day[nd$treatment == "B"], nd$fit[nd$treatment == "B"], type = "b",
      pch = 17, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("A", "B"), pch = c(16, 17), col = c("black", "red"), bty = "n")
days <- sort(unique(cg$day))
nd <- expand.grid(day = days, treatment = factor(c("A", "B")))
nd$fit <- predict(final, newdata = nd, level = 0)
plot(nd$day[nd$treatment == "A"], nd$fit[nd$treatment == "A"], type = "b",
     pch = 16, ylim = range(nd$fit), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Predicted weight (kg)")
lines(nd$day[nd$treatment == "B"], nd$fit[nd$treatment == "B"], type = "b",
      pch = 17, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("A", "B"), pch = c(16, 17), col = c("black", "red"), bty = "n")
Population-level predictions, level = 0, meaning the average animal in each group rather than any particular animal.
The two curves cross, which is what the raw means suggested in week 1. Group A starts heavier and group B overtakes it — a difference in slope, which is exactly what the interaction term encodes.
cattle in each group. Comment on the plots.
Subset to the four animals, use `predict()` for their fitted lines, then overlay
the observed points. Because these are subject-specific predictions, the lines
should track individual animals more closely than the group means did.
pick <- c(1, 2, 31, 32)
sub <- cg[cg$subject %in% pick, ]
sub$fit <- predict(final, newdata = sub)
plot(sub$day, sub$Y, col = factor(sub$subject), pch = 16,
     xlab = "Day", ylab = "Weight (kg)")
for (s in pick) {
  d <- sub[sub$subject == s, ]

Writing the model in matrix form, and seeing why the random slope makes the marginal variance grow with time — animals fan out.

title: Longitudinal data analysis: week 5 tutorial
text:
Week 5 — Generalised estimating equations
\(Y_{ij} \in \{0,1\}\) records whether child \(i\) has a respiratory infection at time \(t_{ij}\), so \(Y_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu_{ij})\) with \(\mu_{ij} = E(Y_{ij}) = P(Y_{ij} = 1)\).
Because \(\mu_{ij}\) must lie in \((0,1)\) while a linear predictor ranges over the whole real line, we need a link function. The natural choice for a binary response is the logit, the canonical link for the Bernoulli:
\[\text{logit}(\mu_{ij}) = \log\!\left(\frac{\mu_{ij}}{1-\mu_{ij}}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}_{ij}
+ \beta_3 \text{Gender}_i + \beta_4 \text{VitA}_{ij},\]
for \(i = 1,\dots,250\) and \(j = 1,\dots,6\).
Interpretation: each \(\beta_k\) is a log odds ratio. In particular \(\exp(\beta_4)\) is the odds of infection for a vitamin A deficient child divided by the odds for a sufficient child, holding time, age and gender fixed. \(\beta_3\) is time-constant (gender does not change), while time, age and vitamin A status vary within a child.
For the variance, a Bernoulli variable has variance determined entirely by its mean — there is no free dispersion parameter:
\[\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = E(Y_{ij}^2) - \{E(Y_{ij})\}^2
= \mu_{ij} - \mu_{ij}^2 = \mu_{ij}(1 - \mu_{ij}),\]
using \(Y_{ij}^2 = Y_{ij}\) for a 0/1 variable. So the variance function is \(v(\mu) = \mu(1-\mu)\), maximal at \(\mu = 1/2\) and shrinking towards zero as \(\mu\) approaches 0 or 1.
In practice one often allows a scale (dispersion) parameter \(\phi\),
\[\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \phi\,\mu_{ij}(1 - \mu_{ij}),\]
with \(\phi > 1\) indicating overdispersion and \(\phi < 1\) underdispersion relative to the Bernoulli. For genuinely binary data \(\phi\) is not identifiable from a single observation, but it becomes meaningful once repeated measurements are pooled, and GEE estimates it as a moment-based scale factor.
What this model does not yet do. It specifies only the mean and the variance of each individual observation. It says nothing about the association between \(Y_{ij}\) and \(Y_{ik}\) for two visits on the same child. Fitting it as though all \(1500\) observations were independent ignores that association — which is exactly what part 2 asks you to do, and what part 3 asks you to repair.
`geese()` (or `geeglm()`) from `geepack`. For "ignoring the correlation", the
working correlation is `corstr = "independence"`.
The response is binary, so `family = binomial`, and `id = ID` tells the function
which rows belong to the same child.
Look at the Wald test for the vitamin A coefficient.

    fit.ind <- geese(Y~Time+age+Gender+VitaminA, id=ID, data=ICHS, family=binomial, corstr='inde')

Extend the model by keeping the same marginal mean but adding a model for the within-child association. This is the generalised estimating equations (GEE) formulation.
Let \(\mathbf{Y}_i = (Y_{i1},\dots,Y_{in_i})^{\mathrm{T}}\) be the responses for child \(i\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i\) the corresponding mean vector. The mean model is unchanged:
\[\text{logit}(\mu_{ij}) = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{\beta}.\]
The covariance of \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) is written as
\[\text{Var}(\mathbf{Y}_i) = \mathbf{V}_i
= \phi\,\mathbf{A}_i^{1/2}\,\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\,\mathbf{A}_i^{1/2},\]
where
Common choices for \(\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\):
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is estimated by solving the estimating equations
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf{D}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{V}_i^{-1}
(\mathbf{Y}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i) = \mathbf{0},
\qquad \mathbf{D}_i = \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathrm{T}}}.\]
Two properties make this worth doing, and they are the heart of the week:
Note that the interpretation of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is marginal — a population-averaged log odds ratio, comparing groups of children — not subject-specific as it would be in a GLMM with random effects. The two are not equal for a logit link, and the distinction matters when reporting.
Try run_app("gee_robustness") to see points 1 and 2 happen: with an exchangeable truth and an independence working correlation, the slope stays unbiased while the naive standard error is badly wrong and the robust one is not.
Refit with `corstr = "exchangeable"`, `"ar1"` and `"unstructured"` in turn.
The point of the exercise is what changes and what does not: compare the
estimates across the four fits, then compare their standard errors.
The estimates should barely move; the standard errors will.

        summary(fit.ar1)

        fit.unstr <- update(fit.ind, corstr="unstructured")
        summary(fit.unstr)
The R outputs above show that the estimates of \(\beta\) are very similar when using different working covariance structures. For the null hypothesis in part (2), they all show that \(\beta_4\) is not statistically significant, which agrees with the conclusion in part (2).
Wei Pan (2001) showed that it is good to use the independent correlation structure in variable selection. Thus, we use the independent correlation structure as working correlation to select covariates below.
The R outputs above show that \(\beta_4\) is not statistically significant, thus we refit model by deleting the covariate :

compare a model with and without it — but note you cannot use a likelihood ratio
test here, because GEE is not likelihood-based. Use the Wald test, or QIC.
